E0126.summary: In Norton's Ordinal, handicraft, the work of the hands, called Art mechanical; what the Gross Work consists of.
E0126.body: A term from Norton's Ordinal, quoted by Atwood: handicraft, “But handie crafte, called Art mechanical,” [IV.1 ¶28]. The record says the Gross Work consists of this handicraft. It is equated there with handie crafte.

E0127.summary: The Art Atwood calls holy above all arts for aiding devout minds; a remedy of imperfect souls offering means of assimilation, though not itself the cause of salvation.
E0127.body: Atwood writes that “The Art of Alchemy is of all Arts distinguished as holt” [IV.4 ¶25] (the spelling is the book's), because it aids devout minds. She adds that “the Art is said to be a remedy of imperfect souls, and offers the means of assimilation” [IV.4 ¶25]. She also holds that the Art is not itself the cause of salvation [IV.4 ¶25].

E0128.summary: The ultimate Art, which Atwood says she will not fully expose and which is to be discovered by a theoretic conduct.
E0128.body: Atwood speaks of discovering, “by a theoretic conduct, the ultimate Art of Life” [IV.2 ¶3]. She does not fully expose this Art; it is to be discovered by a theoretic conduct.

E0129.summary: A concealed practical art which, with the vessel, the ancients are said to have hidden; Atwood names it without explaining it.
E0129.body: Atwood mentions “the concealed vessel or art of vital administration” [II.1 ¶8] among the things the ancients hid. The text does not explain it here; the “or” may present the vessel and the art as alternative names for one concealed thing, or as two things named together; the text does not decide.

E0130.summary: The art said by unnamed others to have been first practised in Egypt by Cham, from whom some derive both the name and the art of alchemy.
E0130.body: Reporting what others say (not her own claim), Atwood records that in Egypt “it was there that the art of Vulcan was first practiced by Cham, one of the sons of the Patriarch” [I.1 ¶5]; some derive both the name and the art of alchemy from Cham.

E0131.summary: Atwood's name for the Art as long called holy, with nothing impure or impious in it.
E0131.body: Atwood writes: “These is nothing impure, or of itself impious, in this Art of Wisdom, long distinguished as holy.” [IV.4 ¶24] (wording as in the book). Compare Art of Alchemy, called holy in the next paragraph [IV.4 ¶25].

E0132.summary: Author of a celebrated treatise on the philosophers' stone whom Atwood quotes at length on long life, secrecy and the non-literal, cabalistic sense of the art.
E0132.body:
Atwood quotes Artephius at length from his celebrated treatise on the philosophers' stone (given in a note as *Artefii Antiquissimi Philosophi de Arte Occulta atque Lapide Philosophorum Liber secretus*) on long life by the quintessence. He says he publishes everything but one point: “I except one thing only, which it is not lawful that I should write, because it can be revealed truly only by God, or by a master” [I.1 ¶27; I.1 ¶36; I.1 n42]. She treats him as a link in alchemy's history as it passed from Asia to Europe [I.1 ¶37].

She cites him with approval to show that the art is cabalistic and must not be read literally: “he that takes the philosophers’ saying according to the outward sense and signification has already lost the clue to Ariadne” [I.1 ¶84; I.1 n108]. Under the spelling Atrephius (*Liber Secretissimus Artefii*) he supports her description of the subject: “a white fume, in substance like to pure silver” [I.2 ¶29; I.2 n28].

With Arnold and Lully he is said to agree with the *Lucerna Salis* description of whitening, as cited earlier “in the Theory” [III.2 ¶5]. As Artefius he is named, with Trevisan and Flammel, among “the sincerest” who passed over the Preparation of Mercury in silence [IV.3 ¶7].

E0133.summary: In Geber, a dissolution according to the course of nature; men's ignorance of it made them think gold-making impossible.
E0133.body: Quoted from Geber: “the artificial destruction according to the course of nature” [II.1 ¶47]. Because men did not know of this dissolution, they thought gold-making impossible.

E0134.summary: The method of the Art, which Atwood says Palingenius divulges in a few lines of verse.
E0134.body: Atwood introduces verses of Palingenius as one who “divulges the artificial method in the few following lines” [III.1 ¶26]. The phrase apparently means the method of the Art itself.

E0135.summary: The practitioner of the Art, who begins, ends and repeats the experiment, but who, according to the theosophist Atwood quotes, cannot do the work and only prepares the way and the matter.
E0135.body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood describes the practitioner: “as the Artist begins, ends, and repeats the mysterious experiment” [APP ¶17].

A theosophist she quotes sets limits on the human operator: “the Artist is not to attempt it --- he cannot do it” [IV.3 ¶38]. The Artist only prepares the way and the matter, and must have understanding and faith [IV.3 ¶38]. The two records differ in emphasis: the Artist as active experimenter, and the Artist as one who cannot do the work alone.

E0136.summary: An authority (spelled thus in the book) cited for deriving Wisdom from clearness and light.
E0136.body: Cited in support of deriving Wisdom from clearness and light: “it is a certain clearness, as being that which renders all things conspicuous” [II.4 ¶26].

E0137.summary: In Norton, the astrological ascendant, which should be direct and fiery and, with its Lord, made fortunate for the operation; a common sign suits the work's many repetitions.
E0137.body: Quoted from Norton: the operation calls for what “Is a direct and Fiery ascendant” [IV.2 ¶34]. The ascendant and its Lord are to be made fortunate. A common sign suits the many repetitions of the work [IV.2 ¶34].

E0138.summary: The prophecy of Egypt's fall in the Asclepian Dialogue; Atwood sees the decline after 640 as something like its fulfilment, only worse than predicted.
E0138.body: Atwood treats the decline after 640 as something like the fulfilment of the Asclepian prophecy, but worse than it predicted [I.1 ¶30]. See Asclepius for the prophecy itself.

E0139.summary: The Asclepian Dialogue of Hermes, a theosophic Hermetic book; Atwood defends as authentic its prophecy of Egypt's fall and cites it on the magicians' original divine power.
E0139.body:
Atwood describes the Asclepian Dialogue of Hermes as a theosophic Hermetic book. It is the source of the prophecy of Egypt's fall: “Oh, Egypt! Egypt! Fables alone shall remain of thy religion” [I.1 ¶7; I.1 ¶10; I.1 n11]. She defends the prophecy as authentic.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she cites the Dialogue, “so called, the 2 nd Book of Hermes, ch. 9”, to support her view that the magicians first drew their power from the Divine Source and later fell into debasement and idolatry [APP ¶5]. See also Asclepian prophecy.

E0140.summary: In Khunrath, what the impure body becomes when consumed and blackened; of great worth, the diadem of the body, holding our pigmy.
E0140.body: Quoted from Khunrath: the impure body, consumed and blackened, becomes ashes, and these are of great worth: “in them lies our pigmy, conquering and subduing giants” [IV.1 ¶36]. He identifies them with the diadem of the body: “they are the diadem of thy body” [IV.1 ¶36].

E0141.summary: Compiler of the Theatrum Chemicum Britanicum, praised by Atwood and cited on secrecy, practical experience, incredulity, the Kelly story and a verse Tablet of Philosophy.
E0141.body:
Atwood praises Elias Ashmole's collection, the *Theatrum Chemicum Britanicum* (London 1652). She cites his preface to show secrecy and the need for practical experience, and also cites him on incredulity as a punishment: “I know enough to hold my tongue, but not enough to speak” [I.1 ¶62; I.1 ¶64; I.1 n66].

Ashmole tells the warming-pan story and judges Kelly more profuse than a sober philosopher should be [I.1 ¶66].

From the *Theatrum* (p. 336, *Experience and Philosophy*) she quotes a verse Tablet erected by Philosophy to Experience: “Blessed be thou, Experience!” [III.3 ¶75; III.3 ¶76; III.3 n49]. It speaks of the One Thing, the first Material Mother and the Three Powers in one seat, which the text at III.3 ¶77 glosses as Sulphur, Mercury and Salt.

E0142.summary: In Synesius, the soul's consent to its purification; without it the soul lacks every purifying machine, assent being the greatest pledge of reconciliation.
E0142.body: Quoted from Synesius: “the soul is deprived of every purifying machine because destitute of assent, which is the greatest pledge of reconciliation” [II.2 ¶13]. The context suggests assent means the soul's own consent to being purified.

E0143.summary: In Boehme, what the new man looks into, equated with the geniture; not further explained.
E0143.body: Quoted from Boehme: the new man looks into “the astral birth or geniture” [III.2 ¶16], which equates it with geniture. The text gives no further explanation.

E0144.summary: A fire said to conquer all things and assimilate them to itself; Paracelsus places it in the tincture, and Eudoxus says the Stone is an Astral Fire.
E0144.body:
Two quoted authorities use the term. Paracelsus speaks of the fire in the tincture: “an astral fire which conquers all things and changes them into a nature like itself” [I.1 ¶76].

Eudoxus identifies the Stone with it: “Our stone is an Astral Fire” [IV.3 ¶16]. He says it sympathizes with Natural Fire and grows, like a Salamander, in Elementary Fire [IV.3 ¶16].

E0145.summary: Atwood's name for the internal spiritual Sun gotten and conceived through the work, which she identifies with a series of traditional images.
E0145.body:
In her own voice Atwood gives a chain of identities: “This is the true Astrum Solis gotten and conceived, the internal spiritual Sun which is the Perpetual Motion of the Wise, and that Saturnian Salt” [II.3 ¶52]. So it is the internal spiritual Sun, the Perpetual Motion of the Wise and the Saturnian Salt.

She goes on: “And this we take to be that midnight Sun of Apuleius, the ignited Stone of Anaxagoras” [II.3 ¶54]; and “This is the triumphal Chariot of Antimony, the Armed Magnet of Helvetius turned swiftly about the current axle of life, which is the Wheel of Fire signalized in Ezekiel” [II.3 ¶54].

The records show it as what the work produces within: something gotten and conceived. Every equation here is Atwood's own.

E0146.summary: An emblem book whose Latin verses Atwood cites in notes to illustrate the one bird as vulture and crow, the egg analogy and the reddening of the whitened water.
E0146.body:
Atwood quotes Latin verses from *Atalanta Fugiens* in her notes as illustrations, not as arguments.

- Emblema xliii shows that the vulture and the crow are one: “Montis in excelso consistit vertice vultur,” [I.3 n12] (ours: On the lofty summit of a mountain stands a vulture).
- Epigramma 8 illustrates the egg analogy: “Est avis in mundo sublimior omnibus, ovum” [I.3 n26] (ours: There is a bird in the world loftier than all, an egg…).
- Emb. xli illustrates the reddening of the whitened water: “Adonis ab apro occuditur, cui Venus occurens tinxit rosas sanquine” [I.3 n54] (ours: Adonis is slain by a boar; Venus, running to him, dyed the roses with blood).

The translations are ours, not the book's.

E0147.summary: The philosophic furnace in which the matter is decocted with continual fire; Hermes' furnace with a glass, the sealed furnace of the Second Operation, less important than the internal Fire.
E0147.body:
A Scholiast calls it “the philosophic furnace called Athanor” [I.3 n57], in which the matter is decocted with continual fire.

Atwood refers to “that Athanor of Hermes before mentioned, or furnace having a glass to it” [II.4 ¶15], “that singular fundamental of his small new world”. She uses it as a comparison for how the Image of Universal Nature is revealed in Elysian intellection.

Eirenaeus subordinates the outer fire to the inner: “be not so careful of the fire of the Athanor as of your internal Fire” [III.1 ¶14]. Khunrath names “one theosophic cabalistically sealed furnace of Athanor” [IV.1 ¶36] for the Second Operation.

E0148.summary: Author of Du Parfait Amour, which Atwood says shows practical knowledge of the art it allegorizes; named among the authors of extant treatises on the stone.
E0148.body: Atwood says Athenagoras's *Du Parfait Amour* shows practical knowledge of the art it allegorizes [I.1 ¶29]. She names him with Heliodorus, Olympiodorus, Synesius, Zosimus and Archelaus as authors of extant treatises on the philosophers' stone [I.1 ¶27; I.1 n34].

E0150.summary: In Vaughan, the material efflux of the soul, which differs from the aerial spirit in constitution only, not in nature.
E0150.body: Quoted from Vaughan: “the aura or material efflux of the soul” [III.3 ¶27]. It differs from the aerial spirit in constitution only, not in nature.

E0151.summary: The gold-making light of the ferment, into whose substance the ferment transmutes everything.
E0151.body: Atwood says the ferment “transmutes all into the substance of its own Aurific Light” [III.1 ¶24].

E0152.summary: In Albertus Magnus, the gold-making principle, identified with fire in the life of all things and strongest in man.
E0152.body: Quoted from Albertus Magnus: “fire, which is the true aurific principle in the life of all” [II.1 ¶12]. This equates the aurific principle with fire, and the record adds that it is strongest in man.

E0153.summary: A living gold-producing seed, the Light that springs from reason's conscious alliance with the higher Cause; the true form of gold, which the covetous spirit cannot quicken.
E0153.body:
Atwood says the seed must be quickened in life, unlike dead metal. The covetous spirit fails at this: “it cannot quicken the aurific seed in life” [III.4 ¶11]. The seed is not further explained in that passage.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she calls it the Light springing from reason's conscious alliance with the higher Cause, which “is the Divine aurific seed and true form of gold.” [APP ¶152]. She also identifies it with the Golden Bough: “That was the Golden Bough which Aeneas carried” [APP ¶152].

E0154.summary: The gold-making substance of life, which the will should return to its source and live there rather than possess.
E0154.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood says the will fails “for want of returning the aurific substance of life into its source and living there” [APP ¶159]. On her account the will should return this substance to its source, not possess it.

E0155.summary: Atwood's gloss: illuminated, by contrariation of its Form.
E0155.body: Atwood glosses the word herself: “aurified --- that is, illuminated by contrariation of its Form” [III.2 n38]. Aurified therefore means illuminated (stated).

E0156.summary: A kind of sulphur, drawn dry from the fountain by the crowned king; Atwood takes it as the multiplicative virtue of the philosophers' stone and a name for the luminous vital principle.
E0156.body:
In the Hermetic passage quoted, the crowned king is described as “drawing from thence the Auripigment dry, without moisture” [I.3 ¶18]. The Hermetic Master's version repeats this: “drawing from thence the Auripigment, dry without moisture” [III.3 ¶17], without defining it.

The same quoted Hermetic material names it among sulphurs: “the auripigment, siretz, and colcothar, which are also sulphur” [I.3 ¶20]. It also identifies the fat of the brain with it: “and of the brain, which too is auripigment” [I.3 ¶20].

Atwood reads it as “that auripigment of philosophers which is the multiplicative virtue of their stone” [I.3 n22]. According to the readers' record she also treats it as a name for the luminous vital principle (no quote given).
